definitions.definition: The buddha without beginning or end, gnosis as its only eye (Nāmasaṃgīti 100).
The non-dual gnosis of immutable bliss and empty form that teaches the Kālacakra; explicitly not a creator.

name: The innate (sahaja) in the Buddhist tantras and dohās

definitions.definition: The co-emergent nature of mind, neither thing nor no-thing, found through the true guru; realized as the one taste of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
The innate joy/gnosis of the fourth moment and consecration; known only by oneself (Hevajra I.8).

relations.standpoint: shared vocabulary of the siddha movements
relations.note: The Nāth, Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyā and Buddhist siddhas share the word and the goal of 'the innate'; each defines it in its own frame (emptiness-bliss here).

name: The non-duality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa

definitions.definition: 'What is saṃsāra is certainly nirvāṇa' (People Dohā v122); not conceiving them as two is the mode of the dharmadhātu (Queen Dohā v10–11).
Union is where saṃsāra and nirvāṇa become one by abandoning the two concepts (Pañcakrama 5.2).
The fifth stage and the goal: union of illusory body and clear light, of the two truths, of generation and completion, of wisdom and compassion; non-dual gnosis, non-abiding nirvāṇa.

relations.note: Union is the culmination of the completion stage.

definitions.definition: Ultimate bodhicitta: free of all entities, aggregates and grasper-grasped, one's own mind unborn (GST 2); conventional bodhicitta the aspiration; in the completion stage also the white drop.

name: The union of wisdom and means (prajñopāya)

definitions.definition: Wisdom (emptiness, feminine) and means (compassion, bliss, masculine) joined — the meaning of 'Hevajra', of the vajra and bell, of deity couples; union is 'knowing the unity of wisdom and compassion' (Pañcakrama 5.7).
Emptiness without compassion is not the supreme path; compassion alone keeps one in saṃsāra; joining the two, one abides in neither (People Dohā v15–17).

Tathāgata (Vairocana), vajra (Akṣobhya), jewel (Ratnasambhava), lotus (Amitābha), action (Amoghasiddhi): the families of the maṇḍala into which aggregates, elements, afflictions and gnoses are ordered; the Guhyasamāja places Akṣobhya at the centre, the yoga tantras Vairocana.
Mirror-like, equality, discriminating, accomplishing and dharmadhātu gnosis: the purified aggregates or afflictions, each of a buddha family; the Yogācāra four plus the dharmadhātu gnosis.

name: The three (four, five) bodies of a buddha in the tantras

definitions.definition: Dharmakāya, saṃbhogakāya and nirmāṇakāya with the svābhāvikakāya; the two form bodies arise through aspiration and compassion (Queen Dohā v64–68).
The generation and completion stages yield the three bodies (Tōh 2292 no. 25); some systems add the body of great bliss.

relations.note: The tantric count includes the Mahāyāna three bodies and adds the essence (and great-bliss) body.

definitions.definition: Cakrasaṃvara (Heruka) in union with Vajravārāhī: the deity couple embodying bliss and emptiness, at the centre of the maṇḍala of the twenty-four sites.
The image arising from emptiness, seen with eyes open or closed like a dream after the ten signs; the cause sealed by immutable bliss.
The unchanging bliss that, joined with empty form, is the goal; bliss that falls away brings dispassion, suffering and death (restricted context).

name: Taking the fruit as the path

definitions.definition: The unsurpassed path of the Mahāyāna's essence takes the fruit as the path and abides as the fruit from the beginning (Queen Dohā v69).

name: The nature of mind in the siddha songs

definitions.definition: Mind itself is the seed of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, like space, beyond colour and shape, unstained by virtue and vice, clear light unobscured by aeons.

relations.note: The siddhas' 'clear light of one's own mind' and the Ārya school's fourth empty are described in the same words (prabhāsvara); the first is pointed out directly, the second reached through the dissolution of winds.

definitions.definition: The fourth empty, all-empty, the cause of the world and the ultimate truth; realized at the fourth stage (abhisambodhi).
Tilopa's clear light of mind; the Ṣaḍdharmopadeśa's clear-light yoga with its appearances.
Empty (light), very empty (light-appearance), great empty (light-attainment) and all-empty (clear light), arising as winds dissolve; the first three with their natural conceptions.

relations.note: Both describe the stages of dissolution of winds into the central channel; the Guhyasamāja's five signs precede the Pañcakrama's empties in the later Tibetan synthesis (not stated in the Indian texts read).

definitions.definition: Thirty-three conceptions of the first empty (from detachment and fear to envy), forty of the second (passion, joy, pride …) and seven of the third (forgetting, confusion …): 160 subtle natures by day and night, moved by wind.

name: The winds as the mount of mind

definitions.definition: Wind is the vehicle of consciousness, five and ten-fold (Pañcakrama 1.3); the natural conceptions run on the winds.
21,600 breaths a day, carried by left and right channels; the middle channel rarely.

name: The four joys (ānanda)

definitions.definition: Joy, supreme joy, joy of cessation and innate joy, arising in consecration and completion-stage yoga as the drop moves through the cakras; the innate is known between supreme joy and cessation (Tilopa) or as the fourth (Saraha).
Saraha warns against identifying the experienced moments with the innate (King Dohā v27).

relations.note: Each joy is paired with one of the four moments.

notes: Order of the third and fourth joys differs between traditions (sahaja placed third or fourth); recorded as such, not reconciled here.

definitions.definition: Variety (vicitra), ripening (vipāka), dissolution (vimarda) and the signless (vilakṣaṇa), paired with the four joys.
Maitrīpa's mahāmudrā: not engaging the mind in concepts — read as the union of clear light and self-consecration, not as mere absence of thought.
All phenomena of one taste in the innate; tastes differ for the unrealized, not for the realized.
The yogin in union sees self and enemy, jewel and chaff, heaven and hell as equal (Pañcakrama 5.30–34).

name: Beings are buddhas obscured by adventitious stains

definitions.definition: Beings are buddhas but covered by adventitious stains; removing them, they are buddhas (Hevajra II.4).
The stain is neither adventitious nor long-lasting, neither born without mind nor abiding in it; it is destroyed by union with emptiness while mind's gnosis-nature remains (Sekoddeśa 129–133).

relations.note: The Hevajra statement echoes the buddha-nature teaching of the Tathāgatagarbha sūtras; the Sekoddeśa's analysis refines the 'adventitious' language.

name: Divine pride (the self as deity)

definitions.definition: In deity yoga the practitioner affirms 'I am of vajra nature', 'as all tathāgatas are, so am I' (Tattvasaṃgraha) — an identity grounded in emptiness, not in a permanent self.

notes: The Tibetan term is standard; a single Sanskrit technical equivalent is not fixed here.

definitions.definition: Scholars do not realize that the buddha is in the body (People Dohā v82); the bodiless hidden in the body (v110); no pilgrimage place equals the body (v57–59); the body is the abode of all buddhas (Advayasiddhi).

relations.note: The siddha motif of the body as the true holy place is shared with Nāth, Tamil Siddha and Sant poetry.

name: The Buddhist subtle body (channels, winds, drops)

definitions.definition: Thirty-two (or 72,000) channels with three principal — lalanā (left, moon), rasanā (right, sun), avadhūtī (centre) — and four (Hevajra) or six (Kālacakra) cakras; winds as the mount of mind; white and red drops; the yoga of drawing the winds into the central channel.
The dohās speak of wind and mind ceasing where sun and moon do not enter (People Dohā v26–27) and of the three channels as bellows and forge (Kamparipa).

relations.note: The Hindu haṭha six-cakra body and the Buddhist four-cakra body share the three channels (the Sekoddeśa itself equates lalanā/iḍā and rasanā/piṅgalā) but differ in the number and meaning of the centres.

name: The four cakras of the Hevajra

definitions.definition: Nirmāṇacakra at the navel, dharmacakra at the heart, saṃbhogacakra at the throat, mahāsukhacakra at the head, correlated with the four bodies and the four joys.
The fierce goddess blazing at the navel who burns the tathāgatas and melts the moon at the crown (Hevajra I.1); first of Tilopa's six dharmas, from Caryāpa.

relations.note: Both are a feminine inner fire/power awakened in the lower body and rising through the central channel; the Buddhist texts frame it as bliss joined with emptiness, not as Śakti uniting with Śiva.

definitions.definition: The self-consecration body of wind and mind, 'like a rainbow in the sky', the conventional truth, obtained only by the guru's grace; joined with clear light in union.
Seeing everything as illusion, dream, mirror-image and painted Vajrasattva (Tilopa, from Nāgārjuna).
The body, speech and mind of all tathāgatas, with OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ, in which the Guhyasamāja opens; purified in the consecrations.

name: The body as the sacred sites

definitions.definition: The twenty-four sites of the Heruka maṇḍala are located inwardly in the body's channels (body maṇḍala); the Hevajra lists the classes of sites.
Saraha: no holy place equals the body (People Dohā v57–59).

name: The aggregates as buddhas, the elements as goddesses

definitions.definition: The five aggregates are the five tathāgatas and the elements their consorts (Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍaravāsinī, Tārā); despising one's aggregates is a root downfall.

notes: Correlations follow the Guhyasamāja scheme as commonly given; they differ between systems.

definitions.definition: The world is bound by passion and freed by passion (Hevajra II.2); the same deeds that bind free when joined with means (Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa 6); as the knower of poison eats poison unharmed (v. 18); 'great passion' is a name of the Buddha.
Tilopa: as one who has taken poison (knowingly) is not killed by it, the yogin is not bound by sense pleasures.
Means that transform what binds into what frees — deity, mantra, bliss — always joined with wisdom.
Pledges taken at consecration — the root and gross downfalls, the pledges of the five families, the vidyādhara vow on top of the prātimokṣa and bodhisattva vows; broken pledges bring the vajra hell.
Tilopa: the vow is the non-conceptual meaning; guarding vows with concepts degenerates from it; Dhūmapa: the supreme vow is not clinging to one's own realization.

name: The fourteen root downfalls

definitions.definition: The fourteen breaches that destroy the tantric pledge, to be memorized after consecration (Gurupañcāśikā 49).

members: not relying on the pledge substances

definitions.definition: The Vajrayāna practitioner holds the monastic or lay prātimokṣa, the bodhisattva vow and the tantric (vidyādhara) vow together; Atiśa forbids celibates the secret and wisdom consecrations to protect the first.

name: The observance of the realized yogin (vratacaryā)

definitions.definition: Unconventional conduct in cremation grounds, among outcastes, with ornaments of bone, 'mad' behaviour and equal vision — undertaken after warmth or realization, as a hidden observance.
Only after realizing equality (Mekopa); the unrealized who act so are like a kingdom seized by its subjects (Nāgārjuna's song); the Queen Dohā describes it and also warns against base conduct.

Disparaging women, who are of the nature of wisdom, is the fourteenth root downfall; the Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa praises women; women siddhas (Lakṣmīṅkarā, Mekhalā, Kanakhalā, Maṇibhadrā, Niguma, Sukhasiddhi) teach.

name: The siddhas' critique of ritual, caste and scholasticism

definitions.definition: Saraha and Tilopa mock Brahmin fire offerings and Vedic recitation, Śaiva ash-smearing, Jain nudity, Buddhist monastic austerity and scholastic learning, pilgrimage and bathing, and even tantric maṇḍala and mantra when taken as ends; the innate is not in them.

relations.note: Parallel critique by the Tamil Siddhars; historical connection not established.

name: The superiority of the mantra way

definitions.definition: Same goal as the perfection way, but superior in being unconfused, rich in means, without hardship and for the sharp-witted.
Generation stage (utpattikrama) and completion stage (utpanna-/niṣpannakrama): the first a staircase to the second; their unity is union.

Arising as the deity: dissolving into emptiness, generating the deity from seed syllables, the maṇḍala, the consecration and sealing, with clarity and divine pride; the Tattvasaṃgraha's five abhisaṃbodhis are its model in the yoga tantras.
Five stages: vajra recitation, mind isolation (the empties), self-consecration, clear light, union.
The six-branch yoga culminating in empty form and immutable bliss.

Meditating oneself as the deity — appearance inseparable from emptiness, with the deity's pride — the distinctive method of the mantra way; 'there is no meditator, no mantra, no deity: mantra and deity abide in the nature free of elaboration' (Hevajra I.5).
Penetrating one's mind, generating bodhicitta, the vajra on the moon disc, making it firm, arising as the Buddha body — Sarvārthasiddhi's awakening in the Tattvasaṃgraha.
The four branches of Guhyasamāja practice (sevā, upasādhana, sādhana, mahāsādhana).

name: Classifications of the tantras

definitions.definition: Indian classes: kriyā, caryā (ubhaya), yoga, yogottara / mahāyoga, yoganiruttara / yoginī (sources vary); the Tibetan fourfold kriyā–caryā–yoga–anuttarayoga with the later father / mother / non-dual subdivision; Nyingma's nine vehicles (outer three, inner three: mahāyoga, anuyoga, atiyoga).

notes: The Indian nomenclature varies across authors (e.g. five- or six-fold lists); the Tibetan fourfold scheme and the father/mother/non-dual labels are later and are labeled as such.

name: The tantric grounds (bhūmi)

definitions.definition: The dohās place realization on 'the fourteenth ground'; the Queen Dohā says grounds, paths and buddhahood are all one innate gnosis.
The Hevajra correlates the ten grounds with ten classes of sacred site; later systems count twelve, thirteen or more grounds.

notes: The numbering systems (13th 'Vajradhara' ground, 14th etc.) belong to later commentaries; not resolved here.

definitions.definition: Tilopa's 'kings': view beyond grasped and grasper, meditation without distraction, conduct without effort, fruit without hope and fear; Lakṣmīṅkarā's sequence realization–meditation–conduct.
Practice is first like a torrent in a gorge, then like the Gaṅgā flowing gently, finally like a river meeting the ocean (Gaṅgāmā v21).
The Queen Dohā closes with the wish that beings attain mahāmudrā by the gradual and the simultaneous entry; the songs also praise instantaneous liberation (Queen Dohā v8).

name: Tilopa's six dharmas (the Indian six yogas)

definitions.definition: Caṇḍālī (Caryāpa), illusory body and clear light (Nāgārjuna), dream (Lavapa), intermediate state and transference (Sukhasiddhi) — the root of the 'six yogas of Nāropa'.

Common siddhis (pacifying, increasing, the eight great siddhis such as the good vase, flight, the sword) and the supreme siddhi (mahāmudrā/buddhahood); Tilopa lists long life, no white hair, radiance and a lion's strength among the signs.
The songs warn against pride in powers and against mistaking experiences for realization.
Mirage, smoke, fireflies, lamp and a cloudless sky arise when the mind enters 'the vajra of cessation' (GST 18.146–149).

name: The ten signs of the Kālacakra

definitions.definition: Smoke, mirage, fireflies, lamp, flame, moon, sun, darkness (Rāhu), the digit (kalā, lightning) and the great drop, after which the universal image of empty form appears (Sekoddeśa 26).

relations.note: The first four signs coincide (order differs: mirage and smoke are swapped) with the Guhyasamāja's five signs.

definitions.definition: The vajra master is inseparable from Vajradhara (Gurupañcāśikā 22), greater than the Buddha in kindness (Pañcakrama 4.2); attainment follows him; to despise him is to despise all buddhas.
The innate is found only from the true guru's mouth; the guru is the boat, the physician, the sun of gnosis.

name: Mutual examination of teacher and disciple

definitions.definition: Before entering the bond, teacher and disciple examine each other, since a broken pledge harms both; a merciless, angry, rigid or boastful person is to be avoided as guru (Gurupañcāśikā 6–7).

name: The qualities of a vajra master

definitions.definition: Steady, disciplined, intelligent, patient, honest, knowing mantra and tantra, compassionate, learned, knowing the ten principles, skilled in maṇḍala and ritual, a teacher of mantra, serene, senses controlled.

Vase, secret, wisdom-gnosis and fourth consecrations, ripening body, speech, mind and gnosis and authorizing the corresponding practices; the higher ones involve restricted yoga; Atiśa forbids them to celibates.
Without the precious consecration one is like an outcaste hoping to be king (Queen Dohā v16).
Seven consecrations 'of the child' (water, crown, ribbon, vajra and bell, great vow, name, permission) and the higher consecrations; three conventional, the fourth ultimate.

The tantras and their coded language are not to be revealed to the unconsecrated or unripe; revealing the secret is a root downfall; one without consecration who practises is 'deceived by the vidyādhara tantras'.

name: Pointing out the nature of mind

definitions.definition: The guru points out mind's nature directly — though 'a finger pointing at the sky does not show the sky' (Queen Dohā v39); 'look and point out reality by yourself in yourself' (v11–12).

name: The eighty-four siddhas

definitions.definition: The canonical list of great adepts in Abhayadatta's lives and the parallel songs of Tōh 2292: men and women of every caste and trade who realized mahāmudrā.

relations.note: The Nāth and Buddhist lists of eighty-four overlap (Mīna/Matsyendra, Gorakṣa, Cauraṅgi, Jālandhara, Kāṇha, Carpaṭi) but are distinct lists.

notes: Tōh 2292's order (read locally) follows Abhayadatta's with a few different names.

name: The seven siddhi texts

definitions.definition: A group of short Indian treatises on the Vajrayāna view (grub pa sde bdun): Padmavajra's Guhyasiddhi, Anaṅgavajra's Prajñopāyaviniścayasiddhi, Indrabhūti's Jñānasiddhi, Lakṣmīṅkarā's Advayasiddhi and others.

notes: The last three members are uncertain; lists differ.

name: The two exegetical schools of the Guhyasamāja

definitions.definition: The Ārya school (Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, Nāgabodhi, Candrakīrti; Akṣobhya maṇḍala; five stages) and the Jñānapāda school (Buddhajñānapāda; Mañjuvajra maṇḍala; the Mukhāgama).

name: The three Indian lineages of Cakrasaṃvara

definitions.definition: Lūipa's, Ghaṇṭāpa's and Kāṇha's (Kṛṣṇācārya's) traditions of Cakrasaṃvara practice.

name: The Vajrayoginī cycles

definitions.definition: Sādhana lineages of Vajrayoginī/Vajravārāhī, notably those of Nāropa (the Nāro Khecarī), Indrabhūti and Maitrīpa, with the 'headless' form linked to Lakṣmīṅkarā and the sisters Mekhalā and Kanakhalā; collected in the Guhyasamayasādhanamālā.

notes: The threefold list (Nāropa, Indrabhūti, Maitrīpa) follows Tibetan presentations; not checked in a text.

definitions.definition: Tilopa received caṇḍālī from Caryāpa, illusory body and clear light from Nāgārjuna, dream from Lavapa, and intermediate state and transference from Sukhasiddhi (Ṣaḍdharmopadeśa, read locally); the Tibetan 'four transmissions' (bka' babs bzhi) name these teachers with varying details.

name: The great monasteries of Indian Vajrayāna

definitions.definition: Nālandā, Vikramaśīla (founded by Dharmapāla, c. 800), Odantapurī, Somapura and Jagaddala, where the tantras were studied, commented upon and conferred (Vikramaśīla's 'gatekeepers' included Nāropa, Ratnākaraśānti and Vāgīśvarakīrti); sacked c. 1200.

notes: Dates and gatekeeper lists from memory (Tāranātha's accounts).

definitions.definition: The tradition identifies the tantric Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva and Candrakīrti with the Madhyamaka masters; the scholarly account places the tantric works c. 9th–10th c. and treats the authors as distinct.
The northern kingdom where the Kālacakra was preserved by King Sucandra and the kalkins; a future kalkin will defeat the barbarian armies and restore the dharma.
The outer wheel of cosmos and time, the inner wheel of the body's channels and breaths (21,600 a day), and the 'other' (alternative) Kālacakra of deity and maṇḍala that purifies the first two.

name: The Kālacakra calendar and the epoch 1027

definitions.definition: The Kālacakra's astronomy and calendar; its sixty-year cycle is reckoned from 1027 CE, the basis of the Tibetan rab byung cycles.

notes: The epoch year as the scholarly account gives it; the tradition reckons from Śambhala.

definitions.definition: Twenty-four sites of India (Pullīramalaya, Jālandhara, Oḍḍiyāna, Arbuda … Kulatā) in three wheels of the Heruka maṇḍala, each with a ḍāka and yoginī; inwardly places of the body.

relations.note: The Buddhist and Śaiva/Śākta pīṭha lists share many names (Oḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri); see brw:saiva-pithas-to-cakrasamvara.

definitions.definition: The Mahāvairocana's Womb (Garbha) maṇḍala of compassion and the Tattvasaṃgraha's Vajradhātu maṇḍala of wisdom, later paired as the 'two maṇḍalas' in East Asia.

name: The three phrases of the Mahāvairocana

definitions.definition: Bodhicitta is the cause, compassion the root, skilful means the culmination; awakening is to know one's own mind as it is.
A as foremost of letters, unborn, the gate of all dharmas (Nāmasaṃgīti; Mahāvairocana; Hevajra); in Advayavajra's reading the 'a' of amanasikāra.

The coded language of tantras and songs; the Hevajra supplies a lexicon; the Pradīpoddyotana reads the tantra by six alternatives; the GST's opening 'bhaga' is glossed as gnosis destroying afflictions.
The Caryāgīti's riddles ('among ten million, could it enter one heart?').
Provisional / definitive, intentional / non-intentional, literal / non-literal: the hermeneutic keys for reading the Guhyasamāja (with the 'seven ornaments').
At death the senses and elements withdraw, the moon, sun and winds gather at the heart, samādhis arise; periods of seven days follow (Tilopa, from Sukhasiddhi).
By habituation earth and the other elements dissolve into awareness and self-appearance becomes mahāmudrā (Caluki).

relations.note: The later synthesis identifies the death process with the stages of the completion stage; the Indian texts read state the parallel only implicitly.

name: Omens of death and cheating death

definitions.definition: Omens read from the flow of winds in the channels; the yogin 'cheats death' by drawing the life-wind into the central channel (restricted).

relations.note: Death omens are catalogued in other systems too.

definitions.definition: U44 contribution: the intermediate state is 'blocked' by deity yoga or resting in reality when turning toward rebirth (Ṣaḍdharmopadeśa, from Sukhasiddhi).
The Sarvadurgatipariśodhana's maṇḍala rites to purify the dead from rebirth in the lower realms, basis of funerary practice in Nepal and Tibet.

Union with a physical consort as a method of the higher consecrations and completion stage; the texts insist on consecration, qualification and non-attachment and warn against mistaking its bliss for the ultimate. Summary only.
Action, dharma, great and pledge seals, from the Tattvasaṃgraha's ritual seals to Advayavajra's stages of realization.

name: The two truths in the tantras

definitions.definition: Self-consecration (illusory body) is conventional truth, clear light ultimate; their union is the goal.
The Buddha teaches by the two truths; three consecrations are conventional, the fourth ultimate.
Female enlightened or worldly beings who reveal instructions (Nāropa's old woman, Virūpa's Nairātmyā), guard the secret and punish breaches.
